question: With a limit of 5, items take mostly 50 ms but one in every five takes 2 s. Why is a worker pool faster than batches of 5 with `Promise.all`?
options: Each batch waits for its 2 s item while four slots sit idle; a pool keeps the other slots processing new items
explanation: Batching forces every group to the speed of its slowest member. A pool refills each slot independently.

question: Your service has a database pool of 10 connections shared by all requests. A nightly job processes 30 000 rows with one query each. Which limit is sensible?
options: A small limit such as 2–3, leaving most connections for user traffic
No limit: the pool queues the extra queries
30 000, so the job finishes as fast as possible
Exactly 10, to use the whole pool
explanation: The job competes with live requests for the same pool. Size its limit from the bottleneck and the share it may take; better still, batch rows into fewer queries.

question: A partner API allows 60 requests per minute. A teammate sets a concurrency limit of 2 and still gets `429` errors. Why?
options: Concurrency is not rate: two slots with 100 ms requests make about 1 200 requests per minute
The pool starts too many workers
explanation: A concurrency cap bounds simultaneous calls, not calls per time window. Rate limits need a token bucket, an interval cap (`p-queue`) or respecting `Retry-After`.
